name: Akamata Snake
description:
Colubrid snake family, genus Dinodon. *Dinodon semicarinatum*

Grows up to about 200 cm. Most easily observed from May through November. The body is
yellowish brown with red-and-black oval crossbands. It has no venom but is aggressive,
hissing and striking if you enter its territory. It feeds on mammals, birds, reptiles,
amphibians, and fish, and even eats sea turtle eggs; it sometimes preys on its natural
enemy, the Habu pit viper. Nocturnal, it can be seen along forest roads and around water,
all the way to the coast. Smaller individuals show stronger red coloring and are very
beautiful, but even a small one gives a painful bite, so take care.

name: Amami Odd-scaled Snake
description:
Takachiho snake family, Takachiho tribe. *Achalinus werneri*

Grows up to about 55 cm. The back is blackish brown or dark brown with a black stripe
running along the midline; the belly is yellow. On Amami it is a legendary snake that you
only encounter under just the right conditions. It sometimes comes to the surface on days
of heavy rain. Nocturnal and subterranean, it lives in forests, grassy areas near water,
and farmland. It feeds on earthworms. It is scarcer and harder to find here than the
Amami odd-scaled snakes on other islands. It is very slender and small, so you may not
notice it even if you drive right past.

name: Pryer's Keelback
description:
Colubrid snake family, genus Hebius. *Hebius pryeri*

Grows up to about 110 cm. Most easily observed from May through November. Slender-bodied,
with a black or blackish-brown color and yellow or brown banding along the body. It
prefers watery habitats and is often found around rice paddies and other spots with
plenty of small frogs. It is venomous, but its fangs for injecting venom are small, and a
bite alone is said not to introduce much venom into the body — even so, the venom itself
is quite potent, so caution is needed. It feeds on frogs, fish, geckos, and small lizards.
It moves quickly, but will threaten you if it senses danger.

name: Habu Pit Viper
description:
Pit viper family, genus Protobothrops. *Protobothrops flavoviridis*

Grows up to about 226 cm, one of the largest snakes on the island. Most active and easiest to
observe from May through November (it may also move on warm days even in winter). Nocturnal,
resting in burrows and crevices during the day. Found from lowland forests to mountain forests,
grasslands, wetlands, farmland, and even trees, and it sometimes enters areas near houses while
hunting rats. Feeds mainly on rats, as well as reptiles, frogs, mammals, and birds. Natural
enemies include the Akamata snake and human hunters. Venomous and highly aggressive. Always
keep a distance of at least 2-3 meters when observing or photographing. If approached, it does
not flee — it immediately takes a striking posture and can lunge roughly two-thirds of its own
body length. A bite deep in the mountains, where there is no phone signal, can become a serious
emergency. Its pattern blends into the forest floor and is very hard to spot; it may be hiding
nearby even when you can't see it. You cannot be too careful.

name: Okinawa Pit Viper
description:
Pit viper family, genus Ovophis. *Ovophis okinavensis*

Grows up to about 80 cm. Cold-tolerant, and on Amami Oshima it can be observed
year-round. Once the rainy season ends and the weather turns hot, it is often seen at
higher elevations. It feeds on small to medium-sized frogs, small mammals, and birds. It
is commonly observed in places with plenty of frogs, such as rice paddies and
slow-flowing streams. A coiled individual barely moves, but it will threaten you if you
enter its territory. It is a venomous snake, so if bitten, go to a hospital immediately.
Be careful not to step on it.

name: Ryukyu Coral Snake
description:
Cobra family, genus Sinomicrurus (also known as the Ryukyu coral snake). *Sinomicrurus
japonicus*

Grows up to about 50 cm. Most easily observed around May and around September. The back
is reddish-brown or orange with five dark brown longitudinal stripes. It is designated a
"Specified Dangerous Animal," a legal category for species considered capable of harming
people. Its venom is neurotoxic and stronger than the Habu's, but its head is small and
its temperament is docile. If picked up, it will jab you with its tail, which is as hard
as bone. It is nocturnal and scarce, so sightings are rare. It is popular enough that some
people visit Amami Oshima specifically hoping to see one.

name: Ryukyu Green Snake
description:
Colubrid snake family, genus Cycophuops. *Cycophuops semicarinatus*

Grows up to about 100 cm. Most easily observed from May through November. Mainly
diurnal, though many individuals are also active at night. It has a small head and feeds
mainly on earthworms, as well as frogs. It is the most numerous snake on Amami Oshima and
can be seen in forests during the day and along forest roads at night. Larger individuals
will sometimes threaten you, but they flee very quickly, sliding down slopes to escape.

name: Amami Rabbit
description:
Rabbit family (Leporidae), genus Pentalagus. *Pentalagus furnessi*

Grows to about 41-51 cm and weighs 1.3-2.7 kg. A species endemic to Japan,
found only on Amami Oshima and Tokunoshima, and often called a "living
fossil" for retaining strongly primitive features. Designated a Natural
Monument in 1921 and a Special Natural Monument in 1963. Nocturnal, it bases
its activity around burrows dug in rock crevices or tree hollows, feeding on
chinquapin nuts and young shoots. Breeding occurs mainly in spring and
autumn, with one young born per litter. Its numbers once declined due to
predation by feral cats and the introduced small Indian mongoose, but as
mongoose eradication efforts have progressed, the population has been
recovering in recent years. It is the emblematic animal of night tours, and
it is not uncommon to encounter one hopping along a forest road.

name: Ryukyu Long-haired Rat
description:
Rat family (Muridae), genus Diplothrix. *Diplothrix legata*

Body length 22-33 cm, tail length 25-35 cm. Japan's largest rat, found only
on Amami Oshima, Tokunoshima, and the northern part of Okinawa Island, with
long bristle-like hairs of 5-6 cm mixed into its coat. Designated a Natural
Monument in 1972 and a Nationally Rare Wild Species in 2016. Nocturnal and
strongly arboreal, it rests during the day in tree-hollow nests lined with
dead leaves. Omnivorous, feeding on chinquapin nuts and insects among other
things. Breeds from autumn into early winter, giving birth to 2-5 young per
litter. It is not very wary, and since it does not flee much even when a
flashlight is shone on it, it can sometimes be observed at leisure along
forest roads.

name: Watase's Shrew
description:
Shrew family (Soricidae), genus Crocidura. *Crocidura watasei*

One of the world's smallest mammals, about 5.5 cm long and weighing just 5-8
g. A species endemic to Japan, found only in the Amami island group (Amami
Oshima, Kakeromajima, Tokunoshima, and others) and the Okinawa Islands. It
prefers open environments such as grassland and farmland, and feeds on small
insects and spiders. Nocturnal, it can sometimes be seen darting quickly
through grassy patches beside forest roads. It differs in habitat from a
forest-dwelling relative of the same genus, and the two are sometimes
confused. It carries no legal capture restriction like a Natural Monument
designation, but it is listed as Near Threatened by the Ministry of the
Environment.

name: Amami Brown Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Rana. *Rana kobai*

Grows to about 3.2-4.6 cm. Breeds from November through January. Lives in forests
and along rivers from lowlands to mountains. Becomes active on humid or rainy days,
and gathers around small ponds and spring-fed pools during the breeding season.
Individuals can also be seen along forest roads. Slender-bodied and reddish brown,
it calls with a sharp "kyok-kyok" note.

name: Amami Green Tree Frog
description:
Tree frog family (Rhacophoridae), genus Zhangixalus. *Zhangixalus amamiensis*

Grows to about 4.5-7.7 cm. Breeds from late December through around May. Found
from lowlands to mountains, in forests around ponds, rice paddies, and other still
water. It calls vigorously on humid or rainy days and lays white, foam-covered egg
masses on branches overhead or in streamside vegetation. Even when calling loudly,
it is very hard to spot. Larger than Hallowell's tree frog, which makes the two
easier to tell apart.

name: Amami Tip-nosed Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Odorrana. *Odorrana amamiensis*

Grows to about 5.6-10.1 cm. Breeds from October through May. Lives around
mountain streams. Slender with good posture, and once you get an eye for it, it
can be recognized even from a distance. Its coloring is rich and varies between
individuals. Designated a Natural Monument in Kagoshima Prefecture, so capturing
or transferring it — including its eggs — is prohibited. Many come out onto
forest roads when it rains, so drive carefully.

name: Amami Spiny Newt
description:
Newt family (Salamandridae), genus Echinotriton. *Echinotriton raffaellii*

Grows to about 14-20 cm in total length. Breeds from around January through
April. Endemic to Amami Oshima, Uke-jima, and Tokunoshima, it lives around
forests and farmland. It becomes active on warm winter days, and during the
breeding season lays eggs under fallen leaves near water. It has a rugged,
blackish-brown body, with orange tints on its rib-tip projections and the ends
of its limbs.

name: Amami Ishikawa's Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Odorrana. *Odorrana splendida*

Grows to about 7.4-13.7 cm. Breeds from late February through around June. Lives
along the gentle headwater streams of mountain areas. Said to be Japan's most
beautiful frog, it is designated a Natural Monument and a Nationally Rare Wild
Species in Kagoshima Prefecture, and capturing or transferring it — including
its eggs — is prohibited. In some spots near higher-elevation streams, its call
can be heard after dark, and at certain locations it can even be seen in summer
when it rains.

name: Amami Sword-tailed Newt
description:
Newt family, genus Cynops. *Cynops ensicauda ensicauda*

Males reach about 14 cm and females about 18 cm in total length. Found on Amami
Oshima, Uke-jima, Kakeromajima, Yoro-jima, and other nearby islands, it breeds
in ponds, rice paddies,
and gentle stretches of streams. After September most individuals leave the
water, and around December, during the breeding season, large numbers can be
observed at the water's edge. It has a black body with yellow or orange spots,
and individual variation is considerable. Okinawa is home to the related
Okinawa sword-tailed newt.

name: Hallowell's Tree Frog
description:
Tree frog family, genus Hyla. *Hyla hallowellii*

Grows to about 3-4 cm. Breeds from March through June. Lives in lowland forests,
thickets, and farmland, and lays eggs in rice paddies and other still water. It
becomes active on humid days and rainy nights, and during the breeding season
forms large chorus gatherings near rice paddies. It perches a little way up, such
as on the tips of branches, and even when calling loudly is hard to spot. Solid
green and very beautiful. Its call resembles that of the Japanese tree frog.

name: Okinawa Rice Frog
description:
Narrow-mouthed frog family, genus Microhyla. *Microhyla okinavensis*

Grows to about 2.2-3.2 cm. Breeds year-round (mainly March through July). Found
in a wide range of habitats from coastal lowlands to mountains, including forest
edges, grasslands, and around houses. Becomes active on humid or rainy days. Its
head is small and its legs are thick, giving it a triangular shape when viewed
from above. Japan's smallest frog, but it calls with a surprisingly loud voice.

name: Otton Frog
description:
Brown frog family, genus Babina. *Babina subaspera*

Grows to about 9-14 cm. Breeds from April through October. Lives mainly in
mountainous areas, but can also be seen in farmland and parks. It becomes active
on humid or rainy days and often comes out onto roads. Males grow larger, making
this Japan's biggest frog aside from the introduced American bullfrog. It has
five toes with a sharp spur on what corresponds to the thumb, thought to be used
by males when fighting each other or during amplexus. Designated a Natural
Monument and a Nationally Rare Wild Species in Kagoshima Prefecture, capturing
or transferring it — including its eggs — is prohibited. It is very large and
impressive, and easy to spot when it comes out onto a road. Its name is said to
come from its call.

name: Ryukyu Kajika Frog
description:
Tree frog family, genus Buergeria. *Buergeria japonica*

Grows to about 2.5-4 cm. Breeds from April through October. Adaptable to
habitats ranging from mountain streams to puddles in built-up areas, it is the
most commonly seen frog on Amami Oshima. It calls especially vigorously on
humid or rainy days. Males are a beautiful yellow, and their call is beautiful
too.

name: Amami Flat Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Dorcus (a subspecies of the flat stag beetle).
*Dorcus titanusu elegans*

A subspecies of the flat stag beetle found in the Amami Islands. It is the most
numerous stag beetle on Amami Oshima. A popular species that grows quite large
in captivity. It gathers at the sap of citrus trees, machilus, chinquapin, and
mallotus trees. In the wild most individuals are under 50mm, and anything over
65mm is quite large. Aim for 70mm+.

name: Amami Lesser Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, subgenus Dorcus (lesser stag beetles). *Dorcus amamianus*

Although its name means "lesser stag beetle," it resembles the Himeoo stag
beetle in many respects. Its mandibles are short and strongly curved, while its
legs and tarsi are long. Active from late May through October. Less numerous
than the lesser stag beetle found on mainland Japan.

name: Amami Roundwing Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Neolucanus (roundwing stag beetles).
*Neolucanus protogenetivus*

Active from around September through October, it can be observed deep in
forests dense with giant Castanopsis sieboldii trees. Collecting is prohibited
under the rare wildlife protection ordinances of five municipalities on Amami
Oshima (including its outlying islands) and three towns on Tokunoshima. To
prevent poaching, cameras have been set up in the mountains, and insect patrols
make rounds during the season. Note: simply taking photographs is fine, but if
you need to enter an area that requires a permit, be sure to apply properly.

name: Amami Mountain Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Lucanus (true stag beetles). *Lucanus ferriei*

Active from around July through September. A rare species found only on Amami
Oshima. Collecting is prohibited by ordinance. Lives in primeval forest above
about 300m elevation. Nocturnal; males can be seen waiting for females high in
trees, but they are hard to spot visually. They are also often seen near the
tops of utility poles. They come to tree sap, fruit traps, and lights, but
collecting them is prohibited.

name: Amami Root Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Aegus (root stag beetles). *Aegus laevicolis subnitidus*

A subspecies of the root stag beetle found in the Amami Islands, and the
largest-growing of Japan's root stag beetle subspecies. Active from around May
through October. It sometimes comes to the sap of machilus, chinquapin,
mallotus, and Albizia trees. In the wild most individuals are around 20mm, and
28mm is considered large. Aim for 30mm+.

name: Amami Sawtooth Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Prosopocoilus (sawtooth stag beetles); Amami
subspecies. *Prosopocoilus dissimilis*

Active from mid-June through early September. Among Japan's sawtooth stag
beetles, those from Amami Oshima are especially large, with long, thick,
imposing mandibles. It frequently flies to citrus trees, mallotus, machilus,
chinquapin, ripe Pandanus fruit and banana traps, and streetlights. Most
individuals are around 60mm, and anything over 75mm is large. Aim for 80mm.

name: Amami Deer Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, genus Rhaetulus (deer stag beetles). *Rhaetulus recticrnis*

Active from around May through September, most easily seen around August.
Collecting is prohibited by ordinance. Areas of relatively higher elevation
offer a better chance of finding it. It is often found on thin branches of
Castanopsis sieboldii or citrus trees. In large individuals the mandibles curve
strongly, like a deer's antlers. Take care not to mistake it for a small
individual of the lesser stag beetle or sawtooth stag beetle and take it home
by accident (never take home an individual you can't identify yourself).

name: Lewis's Horned Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, subfamily Aesalinae (minute stag beetles), genus Nigidius
(horned gourd stag beetles). *Nigidius lewisi*

Glossy all over the body, with distinctively shaped mandibles, it spends the
whole year inside rotten wood. It can be found year-round in fallen oak and
chinquapin logs and under leaf litter. Telling males and females apart is
difficult. On Amami it has a very localized distribution and rarely comes to
tree sap, making it hard to find.

name: Amami Ridged Flat Stag Beetle
description:
Stag beetle family, subgenus Dorcus (flat stag beetles). *Dorcus metacostatus*

Active from late April through around October, peaking in July. A rare species
endemic to Japan, found only in the Amami Islands, with eight distinct ridges
on its elytra. It frequently flies to citrus trees, machilus, mallotus,
chinquapin, banana traps, and streetlights. Anything over 60mm is large — aim
for 70mm+.

name: Red-bellied Long-legged Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Stenelmis. *Stenelmis hisamatsui* M. Satô, 1960

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups and Guam.
Riffle beetles live mainly in clean streams; both larvae and adults spend their
lives in the water, growing to about 5mm at most, and the family is watched as
an indicator of clean rivers. The detailed ecology of this species itself is
still largely unknown.

name: Amami Broadbody Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Dryopomorphus. *Dryopomorphus amami* Yoshitomi & M. Satô, 2005

An endemic species found only on Amami Oshima, described in 2005. The genus
Dryopomorphus also includes a widespread relative found on Honshu, Shikoku,
and Kyushu along with a smaller species, plus another species endemic to the
Osumi Islands. Riffle beetles are mainly small aquatic beetles living in clean
streams, but the detailed ecology of this species itself is still largely
unknown.

name: Amami Groove Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Ordobrevia. *Ordobrevia amamiensis* (Nomura, 1957)

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami, Okinawa, and Yaeyama island groups
and Guam. The population on Okinawa Island is distinguished as a separate
subspecies, the Okinawa groove riffle beetle. Riffle beetles mainly live in
clean streams, but the detailed ecology of this species itself is still
largely unknown.

name: Amami Sidegroove Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Leptelmis. *Leptelmis torikaii* Kamite, Yoshitomi & Hayashi, 2017

Endemic to Amami Oshima, a species described as recently as 2017. Its form
differs from other species in the same genus found on mainland Japan and
Taiwan, while the shape of its genitalia, among other features, closely
resembles a species distributed in southern China, indicating a close
relationship. It is regarded as an example of a relict endemic species: its
ancestral species is thought to have once been widespread across the Eurasian
continent, and after Amami Oshima became isolated, related populations
elsewhere died out, leaving only this species surviving. Riffle beetles are
mainly small aquatic beetles living in clean streams, but the detailed ecology
of this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Brown Micro Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Microvelia. *Microvelia japonica*
Esaki & Miyamoto, 1955

A small aquatic insect about 1.5-2.1mm long. Found on Honshu (west of
Fukushima Prefecture), Shikoku, and Kyushu, and in the Ryukyu Islands from
Kikaijima to Okinawa Island. Commonly seen in dim pools beside small streams
and in the shade of rocks, where it preys on small insects that fall onto the
water's surface.

name: Iriomote Micro Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Microvelia.
*Microvelia iriomotensis* Miyamoto, 1964

A small aquatic insect about 1.7-1.9mm long. Found in the Ryukyu Islands
(from the Amami group to the Yaeyama Islands) and Taiwan. Seen in pools formed
by seepage beside mountain forest roads; a mating behavior in which males
guard females for extended periods has been reported in academic research.

name: Common Micro Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Microvelia. *Microvelia douglasi*
Scott, 1874

About 1.5-2mm long, one of the smallest of the broad-shouldered water
striders. Found on Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, Tsushima, the Ryukyu Islands, and
the Daito Islands (Minami Daito-jima), and more widely abroad from the Korean
Peninsula through China, Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and Oceania. It prefers
flowing water such as small rice paddies and streams, and preys on small
insects that fall onto the water's surface. The family includes both wingless
forms that cannot fly and long-winged forms that can.

name: Lesser Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Cybister. *Cybister tripunctatus orientalis*
Gschwendtner, 1931

Grows to about 24-29mm. Found on Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu, the Ryukyu Islands,
and the Ogasawara Islands, and abroad in China, the Korean Peninsula, and
Taiwan. Elongate-oval and somewhat flattened, with a strongly glossy back
ranging from green to brownish black; a yellow rim along the edge of the
elytra is the key point for telling it apart from the tawny diving beetle. It
lives in ponds and marshes rich in aquatic plants, rice paddies and nearby
puddles, fallow fields, and slow-moving channels. Since the 1960s it has
declined sharply on Honshu and further south due to pesticide use and field
consolidation, and is listed as Vulnerable on the Ministry of the
Environment's Red List, but it is still relatively commonly seen in the
Ryukyu Islands. It closely resembles the tawny diving beetle in shape and
coloring, making the two difficult to tell apart from photographs alone.

name: Elongate Glossy Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Zaitzevia. *Zaitzevia elongata* Nomura, 1962

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups. Eight
species of the genus Zaitzevia are known in Japan, with different species
distributed from Honshu to the Yaeyama Islands. Riffle beetles mainly live in
clean streams, but the detailed ecology of this species itself is still
largely unknown.

name: Nomura's Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Stenelmis. *Stenelmis amami* Yoshitomi et Hayashi, 2021

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups. It was
originally treated as the sole species of its own genus, but a 2021 molecular
phylogenetic study (Kobayashi et al., 2021) placed it in the genus Stenelmis.
The genus name (Nomuraelmis) and the Japanese common name were coined in
1964 by Dr. Masataka Satô, and are thought to honor Dr. Nomura, who helped
pioneer riffle beetle research in Japan during that same era.
The detailed ecology of this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Okinawa Striped Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Hydaticus. *Hydaticus vittatus* (Fabricius, 1775)

Grows to about 11-14mm. A southern-type diving beetle found in the Ryukyu
Islands south of Yakushima, and abroad in Taiwan, China, and Southeast Asia.
Lives in still water such as ponds and rice paddies rich in aquatic plants.
In addition to habitat decline, many diving beetles, including this species,
have recently been found being sold for what appears to be the pet trade, so
in January 2023 it was designated, along with other diving beetles, a
Specified Second-Class Nationally Rare Wild Species. This designation only
regulates capture and transfer for the purpose of sale or distribution;
capturing it for observation is not restricted. It closely resembles a
related species of the same genus distributed west of Honshu, but the two
are easy to tell apart since their ranges do not overlap.

name: Ryukyu Broadchest Glossy Beetle
description:
Long-toed water beetle family (Dryopidae), genus Elmomorphus.
*Elmomorphus amamiensis* Nomura, 1959

A small aquatic beetle recorded on Amami Oshima and Okinoerabujima. It was
formerly treated as a Ryukyu-island subspecies of a mainland species, but in
2014 a study using COI gene sequencing and morphological comparison found a
major genetic divergence at the species level between the two, and it was
elevated to full species status. It is now generally accepted as a distinct
species. The Dryopidae are a family closely related to the riffle beetles
(Elmidae) and likewise live in clean streams. The detailed ecology of this
species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Sato's Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Sinonychus. *Sinonychus satoi* Yoshitomi & Nakajima, 2007

A small aquatic beetle found in the Amami and Okinawa island groups (no record
from Okinawa Island itself), described in 2007. Only two species of the genus
Sinonychus are known in Japan; the other is found in Kyushu. The detailed
ecology of this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Tsutsui's Stream Water Strider
description:
Broad-shouldered water strider family, genus Pseudovelia (stream water
striders). *Pseudovelia tsutsuii* Esaki & Miyamoto, 1955

Found in the Ryukyu Islands (from Takarajima to Okinawa Island). Several
species of the genus Pseudovelia are known in Japan, a group that lives along
the banks of rivers and ponds. Sufficient information on the detailed ecology
of this species itself has not yet been confirmed.

name: Ueno's Glossy Riffle Beetle
description:
Riffle beetle family, genus Urumaelmis. *Urumaelmis uenoi* (Nomura, 1961)

A small aquatic beetle found in the Osumi Islands, Tokara Islands, Amami
island group, and Okinawa island group. The genus Urumaelmis also includes a
second species newly described from Kyushu in 2020, bringing the number of
known species in Japan to two. The population on Kuchinoshima in the Tokara
Islands is distinguished as a separate subspecies. The detailed ecology of
this species itself is still largely unknown.

name: Pale Striped Diving Beetle
description:
Diving beetle family, genus Hydaticus (striped diving beetles).
*Hydaticus rhantoides* Sharp, 1882

A small diving beetle about 10-11mm long. The elytra are overall yellowish
brown with no conspicuous striping. Found on Honshu (west of the Kanto
region), Shikoku, Kyushu, Tsushima, the Ryukyu Islands, and the Daito Islands,
and abroad in China, Taiwan, and Southeast Asia. Lives in open still water
such as rice paddies and ponds. Among the diving beetles of the Ryukyu
Islands, it is considered, along with the tawny diving beetle and the lesser
diving beetle, to be relatively holding its own in numbers.

name: Barbour's Skink
description:
Skink family (Scincidae), genus Plestiodon. *Plestiodon barbouri*

Total length 15.5-20 cm (snout-vent length 5.2-7.3 cm). A species endemic to
Japan, distributed on Amami Oshima, Kakeromajima, Uke-jima, Yoro-jima,
Tokunoshima, and the Okinawa Islands. Juveniles are blackish brown with five
bright longitudinal stripes, and a vivid blue tail that makes up more than
two-thirds of the total tail length. As they grow, the blue fades; males
become overall dark brown to brown, while many females retain coloring
closer to that of juveniles. It prefers the forest floor and edges of
natural evergreen broadleaf forest or well-recovered secondary forest,
basking in the sun to regulate its body temperature while feeding on
spiders and land snails. It becomes sluggish in winter but does not
hibernate. Its numbers have declined due to drying of habitat from logging
and undergrowth clearance, and predation by feral cats and the introduced
small Indian mongoose. It is listed as Vulnerable on the Ministry of the
Environment's Red List, and in 2019 was also designated a Kagoshima
Prefecture Rare Wildlife Species, making unauthorized capture or collection
subject to penalties.

name: Ryukyu Robin
description:
Old World flycatcher family (Muscicapidae), genus Larvivora.
*Larvivora komadori*

About 14 cm long, weighing about 18 g. A species endemic to Japan that
breeds from the Danjo Islands through the Tokara Islands, Amami Oshima and
its surrounding islets, to Tokunoshima; designated a Natural Monument in
1970. Males have a vivid orange-red head, back, and tail, and the black
patches on the breast and flanks look like a "beard," which gives the
species its Japanese name. Females are overall plainer in color. It forages
for insects on the forest floor of evergreen broadleaf forest, proclaiming
its territory with a strong, beautiful song. It is easiest to find early in
the morning by following its song. A different species lives in northern
Okinawa Island, but the two ranges do not overlap.

name: Amami Woodcock
description:
Sandpiper family (Scolopacidae), genus Scolopax. *Scolopax mira*

About 35-36 cm long. A species endemic to Japan found only in the Amami and
Okinawa island groups, with breeding confirmed on Amami Oshima, Kakeromajima,
Uke-jima, Yoro-jima, and Tokunoshima. It resembles the closely related
Eurasian woodcock but has longer legs, an overall blacker tone, and a
stockier build than other sandpipers. It prefers the dim forest floor of
evergreen broadleaf forest, is most active from dusk to dawn, and forages on
the ground for earthworms and insects. It becomes especially active in the
dim light of early morning and evening, and on moonlit nights. It nests on
the ground within forests and lays 2-4 eggs from around March through May.
Designated a Nationally Rare Wild Species in 1993. Predation by mongooses
and feral cats, along with habitat loss from logging, are ongoing concerns.

name: Amami Thrush
description:
Old World flycatcher family (Muscicapidae), genus Zoothera.
*Zoothera dauma major*

About 30 cm long. A resident bird found only on Amami Oshima, with a
yellowish-brown ground color marked with black, tiger-like blotches.
Designated a national Natural Monument and a Nationally Rare Wild Species.
It prefers the dim forest floor of mature broadleaf forest and feeds on
earthworms and the like. During the breeding season from February to early
April, it sings a clear, beautiful "kyoroon, tsi-i" call in the dim light
before dawn and at dusk. It once declined so sharply due to logging and the
impact of invasive species that it was called a "phantom bird," but as the
forest has recovered, its population has been on a recovering trend in
recent years.

name: Owston's Woodpecker
description:
Woodpecker family (Picidae), genus Dendrocopos.
*Dendrocopos leucotos owstoni*

About 28 cm long, a medium-sized woodpecker. An endemic subspecies found
only on Amami Oshima; the upper body is almost entirely black with white
spots, and the underside is a stronger brown than in other subspecies. The
crown is red in males and black in females, making the sexes easy to tell
apart. It lives mainly in mature laurel forest and excavates nest holes in
the trunks of large broadleaf trees. It feeds mainly on longhorn beetle
larvae hidden in rotten wood. Territorial proclamations and courtship
displays begin around winter, and from February through May its
"drumming" — rapid pecking at a trunk with its bill — and calls are easiest
to hear. In recent years its range has expanded across the whole of Amami
Oshima, partly due to the effects of pine wilt disease. Since the only
other woodpecker on Amami Oshima is the Amami pygmy woodpecker, the two can
be told apart by size alone. Designated a national Natural Monument in 1971
and a Nationally Rare Wild Species in 1993; capture and transfer are
prohibited.

name: Lidth's Jay
description:
Crow family (Corvidae), genus Garrulus. *Garrulus lidthi*

About 38 cm long. A species endemic to Japan found only on Amami Oshima,
Kakeromajima, and Uke-jima, beautiful with its azure-blue body, reddish-brown
wings, and white bill and wingtips. Designated a Natural Monument in 1921.
It prefers evergreen broadleaf forest and is omnivorous, feeding on
chinquapin and oak acorns. Breeds from around February through May, laying
3-7 eggs in a tree hollow or similar site. Its numbers once declined due to
predation by feral cats and the introduced small Indian mongoose, but
conservation efforts have paid off — including the 2024 declaration of
mongoose eradication — and its population has been recovering in recent
years. It flies about actively during the day, but at night it can be
observed resting on power lines or branch tips along forest roads.
